title: PWM & RGB LEDs: Colors and Brightness
summary: Journey from ON/OFF to variable output using PWM, control brightness, and mix colorful light with RGB LEDs.

steps.title: From ON/OFF to Control
steps.markdownContent:
Imagine you are building a robotic monster in the dark! So far, your digital output pins act like a standard light switch on the wall: they can only be completely **ON (+5V)** or completely **OFF (0V)**.

When you call `digitalWrite(pin, HIGH)`, the light turns on at full power. When you call `digitalWrite(pin, LOW)`, the light switches off entirely.

```
Digital Output:  0V (LOW / OFF)  ⟷  5V (HIGH / ON)
```

What if your monster wants to wake up slowly with a gentle dawn glow? What if you want a soft nightlight, a pulsing heartbeat beacon, or smooth motor speed control instead of full-throttle jerking?

In the physical world, things do not simply snap between 0% and 100%. We need **variable control**—the ability to choose any brightness between total darkness and full blast!

Microcontrollers do not have built-in dials that turn voltage down to 2.5V or 1.2V on their digital pins. So how can a digital chip that only speaks 0s and 1s create smooth, gentle brightness?

Get ready to discover the magic trick of electronics: **Pulse Width Modulation (PWM)**!

quickCheck.question: What happens when an Arduino digital output pin is set to HIGH?
options: It connects to the full +5V supply rail (turned ON)
It drops the voltage to half-power (+2.5V)
It disconnects power and turns off the circuit
quickCheck.explanation: A digital HIGH connects the pin to the full +5V supply rail, turning the output completely ON.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Digital pins have two states: HIGH means ON (+5V) and LOW means OFF (0V).

quickCheck.question: If you want an LED connected to an output pin to turn completely dark, what command state do you send?
quickCheck.explanation: Sending LOW switches the pin to 0V (Ground level), stopping current and turning off the LED.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: In digital electronics, LOW means 0 Volts, which turns off power to components.

steps.title: What Is PWM?
steps.markdownContent:
**Pulse Width Modulation (PWM)** is the clever engineering technique microcontrollers use to simulate variable brightness using only digital ON and OFF signals!

Here is the secret: instead of lowering the voltage, the Arduino flips the pin ON and OFF hundreds of times every single second (about 490 to 980 times per second)!

Why doesn't the LED look like a flickering strobe light?
Because of a property of human vision called **Persistence of Vision** (flicker fusion). Your eyes and brain can only process about 60 image updates per second. When an LED flickers at 490 times per second, the flashes blur together!

Your eyes integrate the bursts of light:
- If the LED is ON for tiny slivers of time and OFF most of the cycle, your brain perceives a **dim, gentle glow**.
- If the LED is ON most of the cycle and OFF for only tiny moments, your brain perceives **bright light**.

It is like flipping a light switch on and off at superhero speed!

quickCheck.question: When a light flashes on and off hundreds of times every second, how do human eyes perceive it?
options: As a steady, smooth glow without visible flickering
As slow, separate flashes that can be counted
quickCheck.explanation: Because our eyes blend fast light pulses together (persistence of vision), rapid flashing appears as a continuous steady glow.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: When light blinks faster than ~60 times a second, our eyes cannot see the flicker and blend it into a steady glow.

quickCheck.question: Does a standard digital output pin physically change its DC voltage to 2.5V, or does it rapidly pulse between 0V and 5V?
options: It rapidly pulses between 0V and 5V to simulate an average voltage
It physically steps down its DC voltage to 2.5V
It changes the chemical composition of the wire
quickCheck.explanation: Digital pins only output 0V or 5V; they create in-between brightness by rapidly pulsing between the two states.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Microcontrollers are digital: they only output 0V (OFF) or 5V (ON). To get medium brightness, they pulse!

steps.title: Duty Cycle
steps.markdownContent:
To control how bright the LED appears, we adjust the **Duty Cycle**.

The duty cycle is simply the **percentage of time** that the signal stays ON (+5V) during each repeating pulse cycle:

- **0% Duty Cycle**: The signal is ON 0% of the time (always 0V). The LED is completely **OFF**.
- **25% Duty Cycle**: The signal is ON for 1/4 of the time and OFF for 3/4 of the time. The LED glows **dimly**.
- **50% Duty Cycle**: The signal is ON half the time and OFF half the time. The LED shines at **medium brightness**.
- **75% Duty Cycle**: The signal is ON 3/4 of the time and OFF 1/4 of the time. The LED shines **brightly**.
- **100% Duty Cycle**: The signal is ON 100% of the time (always +5V). The LED shines at **maximum brightness**!

```
 0% Duty:  ____________________________________ (OFF)
25% Duty:  _--________--________--________--___ (DIM)
50% Duty:  _----____----____----____----____--- (MEDIUM)
75% Duty:  _------__------__------__------__--- (BRIGHT)
100% Duty: ------------------------------------ (MAX)
```

The width of the ON pulse determines the brightness. That is why it is called **Pulse Width Modulation**—we modulate (adjust) the width of the pulse!

quickCheck.question: If an electrical signal spends half of each cycle turned ON and half turned OFF, what is its duty cycle?
quickCheck.explanation: Spending half the time active and half inactive corresponds to a 50% duty cycle.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Duty cycle is the percentage of ON time: half of 100% is 50%.

quickCheck.question: What happens to the perceived brightness of an LED as its ON-time percentage increases?
quickCheck.explanation: More time ON during each cycle delivers more light energy to your eyes, making the LED appear brighter.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: The longer the pulse stays ON during each cycle, the brighter the light appears.

steps.title: LED Brightness
steps.markdownContent:
Let's wire an LED circuit and examine how hardware components protect your circuit!

### Circuit Building Steps:
1. **Identify LED Polarity**:
   - The **Anode** (positive) is the **longer leg**.
   - The **Cathode** (negative) is the **shorter leg** (and has a flat edge on the plastic collar).
2. **Add a Current-Limiting Resistor**:
   - Connect a **220Ω resistor** (color bands: red-red-brown-gold) in series with the LED.
   - *Why?* LEDs have almost no electrical resistance once illuminated! Without a resistor, excessive current rushes through the delicate semiconductor, overheating and damaging it. The resistor keeps current safely below 20 mA.
3. **Connect to Arduino**:
   - Connect the resistor to **Digital Pin ~9** (a PWM pin marked with a tilde `~`).
   - Connect the short leg (Cathode) to **GND** (Ground).

```
Pin ~9 ──[ 220Ω Resistor ]──( Anode + ) LED ( - Cathode )── GND
```

When testing brightness, remember: changing pulse width changes perceived brightness, while the resistor keeps current safe!

quickCheck.question: Why is a current-limiting resistor required in series with an LED?
options: To limit electrical current and protect the LED from burning out
To change the color of the emitted light
To increase the microcontroller clock speed
quickCheck.explanation: Without a resistor, excessive current flows through the LED diode junction, causing overheating and permanent damage.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: LEDs need a resistor to restrict current flow and keep components safe.

quickCheck.question: When inspecting a standard LED, which lead connects toward Ground (0V)?
options: Either leg—LEDs work in both directions
quickCheck.explanation: The shorter leg with the flat notch is the cathode (negative terminal) and connects toward Ground.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Diodes only allow current to flow in one direction! Long leg is positive (anode), short leg is negative (cathode).

steps.title: analogWrite

quickCheck.question: What symbol on the Arduino Uno printed silkscreen marks digital pins that support PWM output?
quickCheck.explanation: Pins marked with a tilde (~) such as 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, and 11 support hardware PWM output.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Look at the digital pin headers on your Arduino board: the wavy line ~ marks PWM pins.

quickCheck.question: In the Arduino analogWrite(pin, value) command, what value produces full 100% brightness?
quickCheck.explanation: analogWrite uses an 8-bit scale from 0 (OFF) to 255 (maximum 100% duty cycle).
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Arduino PWM operates on an 8-bit scale: 0 is completely off, and 255 is maximum power.

steps.title: Meet the RGB LED
steps.markdownContent:
Single-color LEDs are great, but monster robots love rich, vibrant color! Meet the **RGB LED**.

### Three Lights in One Package
An RGB LED looks like a single frosted bulb, but inside the lens are **three separate semiconductor dies**:
- One **Red** LED
- One **Green** LED
- One **Blue** LED

### The 4-Leg Tour:
Because there are three LEDs inside, how many wire legs does the component have? **Four legs!**
Each color has its own control leg, and all three share one common pin:

1. **Leg 1 (Outer Left)**: Red Anode
2. **Leg 2 (Longest Leg)**: Common Pin (Cathode / GND on Common Cathode LEDs)
3. **Leg 3**: Green Anode
4. **Leg 4 (Outer Right)**: Blue Anode

```
   [Frosted 5mm Lens]
        │ │ │ │
        │ │ │ └── Leg 4: Blue
        │ │ └──── Leg 3: Green
        │ └────── Leg 2: Common (Longest!)
        └──────── Leg 1: Red
```

### Three Dedicated Resistors!
**Golden Rule**: Always connect a separate 220Ω resistor to EACH color leg (Leg 1, Leg 3, and Leg 4)!
*Why not share one resistor on the common leg?*
Red LEDs operate around ~2.0V, while Green and Blue operate around ~3.2V. If you share one resistor, the lower-voltage Red channel draws all the current, causing Green and Blue to dim or turn off!

quickCheck.question: How many physical wire legs does a standard single-package RGB LED have?
quickCheck.explanation: An RGB LED has 4 legs: one control leg for each of the 3 colors, plus one shared common leg.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Three color channels plus one common shared pin equals 4 legs total on an RGB LED.

quickCheck.question: Why should each color channel of an RGB LED have its own dedicated series resistor?
options: Because Red, Green, and Blue have different operating voltages and need independent current regulation
To convert the LED into a sensor
quickCheck.explanation: Dedicated resistors ensure each color channel receives balanced current without stealing power from adjacent channels.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Red, green, and blue LEDs use different forward voltages. A resistor for each color keeps all three balanced and protected.

steps.title: Mixing Colors
steps.markdownContent:
Mixing light is pure physics magic!

When you mix paint in art class (subtractive color), combining colors absorbs wavelengths, eventually creating muddy dark brown or black.

With light, we use **Additive Color Mixing**. When colored light beams overlap, they add energy together:

- **Red + Green = Yellow** (Red and green light beams combine into bright yellow!)
- **Green + Blue = Cyan** (Vibrant aqua / sky blue)
- **Red + Blue = Magenta** (Vivid purple / hot pink)
- **Red + Green + Blue = White** (All three primary wavelengths create clean white light!)

### Creating Custom Shades with PWM:
By varying the PWM values between 0 and 255 on each channel, you can blend any shade imaginable:
- **Orange**: High Red (`255`) + Medium-Low Green (`80`) + Zero Blue (`0`)
- **Purple**: Medium Red (`160`) + Zero Green (`0`) + High Blue (`255`)
- **Soft Pink**: Full Red (`255`) + Low Green (`80`) + Low Blue (`80`)

With $256 \times 256 \times 256$ possible combinations, your Arduino can synthesize over **16.7 million distinct colors**!

quickCheck.question: In additive light color mixing, what color do you see when Red light and Green light shine together at equal brightness?
quickCheck.explanation: In additive light physics, combining pure Red and Green beams creates bright Yellow light.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Light mixing is additive! Unlike paint, combining red light and green light shines as bright yellow.

quickCheck.question: What color is created when Red, Green, and Blue light all shine simultaneously at full brightness?
quickCheck.explanation: Combining all three primary light wavelengths (Red, Green, Blue) at full intensity produces White light.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: When all three light channels are turned on at full power, their wavelengths blend to form White light.

steps.title: Common Cathode vs Common Anode
steps.markdownContent:
When using an RGB LED, you must know which internal wiring standard it uses: **Common Cathode** or **Common Anode**.

### 1. Common Cathode (Standard in Monster Lab Kits)
- **Cathode** means negative terminal (GND).
- The longest shared pin connects to **GND (0V)**.
- Driving a color pin HIGH (or positive PWM) turns that color **ON**.
- `analogWrite(redPin, 255);` = 100% Brightness.
- `analogWrite(redPin, 0);` = Completely OFF.
- *Straightforward and intuitive logic!*

### 2. Common Anode
- **Anode** means positive terminal (+5V).
- The longest shared pin connects to **+5V**.
- Driving a color pin LOW (0V) completes the circuit and turns that color **ON**.
- `analogWrite(redPin, 0);` = 100% Brightness!
- `analogWrite(redPin, 255);` = Completely OFF!
- *Inverted logic (Active-LOW)!*

### Quick Hardware Test:
Plug the longest pin into GND. Touch a 220Ω resistor from 5V to any color pin. If that color lights up, congratulations—you have a **Common Cathode** LED!

quickCheck.question: In a Common Cathode RGB LED, what does the shared longest pin connect to?
quickCheck.explanation: Cathode is the negative terminal, so a Common Cathode LED shares a single connection to Ground (GND).
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Cathode means negative (GND), while Anode means positive (+5V). Common Cathode connects to GND.

quickCheck.question: If an RGB LED has Common Anode wiring (shared +5V), what code value turns a color channel fully ON?
options: 0 (or LOW), because current flows when the pin is pulled down to 0V
quickCheck.explanation: Common Anode LEDs use inverted (active-LOW) logic: sending 0 connects the pin to Ground, completing the circuit from +5V.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Common Anode has inverted logic: pulling a pin to 0V turns it ON, and sending 255 turns it OFF.

steps.title: RGB Mini Project

quickCheck.question: Which set of Arduino Uno pins is used for PWM color control in this project?
quickCheck.explanation: Pins ~9, ~10, and ~11 all feature hardware PWM (tilde ~), allowing variable brightness on every color channel.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Look for the tilde (~) on the Uno silkscreen: pins 9, 10, and 11 all support PWM.

quickCheck.question: In the setColor(red, green, blue) function, what arguments produce a bright Yellow status light?
quickCheck.explanation: Yellow light is synthesized by mixing Red and Green while keeping Blue turned off.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: To create yellow light, turn ON Red (255) and Green (255), and set Blue to 0.

interactiveConfig.question: What is the primary purpose of Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) when controlling an LED?
options: To simulate variable brightness by rapidly pulsing between ON and OFF
To convert the LED into a digital temperature sensor
To make the Arduino run at double clock speed
interactiveConfig.explanation: PWM rapidly pulses a digital output so human eyes perceive smooth, variable brightness.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) when controlling an LED?
options: To simulate variable brightness by rapidly pulsing between ON and OFF
To convert the LED into a digital temperature sensor
To make the Arduino run at double clock speed
questions.explanation: PWM rapidly pulses a digital output so human eyes perceive smooth, variable brightness.

questions.question: What duty cycle percentage produces medium (approximately half) brightness on an LED?
questions.explanation: A 50% duty cycle powers the LED for half the pulse duration, creating roughly half brightness.

questions.question: What integer value in analogWrite(pin, value) corresponds to full 100% brightness?
questions.explanation: analogWrite is 8-bit, so values range from 0 (OFF) to 255 (full 100% duty cycle).

questions.question: Which pins on an Arduino Uno support hardware PWM output?
options: Pins marked with a tilde (~) such as 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, and 11
Only analog pins A0 through A5
questions.explanation: Only pins marked with a tilde (~) on the Uno silkscreen support PWM output.

questions.question: Why does an RGB LED need a separate resistor on each color channel?
options: Because Red, Green, and Blue have different forward voltages and each need dedicated current limiting
To change the frequency of the microcontroller oscillator
To convert alternating current into direct current
questions.explanation: Independent resistors ensure safe current distribution across colors with different forward voltage drops.

questions.question: In additive light mixing, what color is created when Red and Green light shine at full intensity?
questions.explanation: In additive color optics, combining red light and green light produces yellow light.

questions.question: Where does the longest lead of a Common Cathode RGB LED connect?
questions.explanation: The cathode is negative, so a Common Cathode LED connects its longest shared lead to Ground (GND).

questions.question: If your RGB LED shows Cyan when you commanded Red, what is the most likely cause?
options: The LED is Common Anode, so its logic is inverted (Active-LOW)
The Arduino has run out of memory
The breadboard is too close to a magnet
questions.explanation: Common Anode LEDs turn ON with LOW (0) and OFF with HIGH (255), so an un-inverted Red command leaves Green and Blue ON (producing Cyan).

quickCheck.question: What happens if you run analogWrite(8, 128) on digital pin 8 on an Arduino Uno?
options: Pin 8 lacks PWM (~), so it will only switch ON or OFF without smooth dimming
Pin 8 will output a continuous analog sine wave
quickCheck.explanation: Pin 8 is not a PWM pin, so analogWrite acts like a simple threshold switch rather than pulsing.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Always check for the tilde (~)! Non-PWM pins cannot dim with analogWrite.

quickCheck.question: In a Common Cathode RGB LED, what code turns both Red and Blue ON to create vibrant Magenta (purple) light?
quickCheck.explanation: Magenta is made of Red plus Blue; with Common Cathode, 255 turns a channel full ON while 0 keeps Green OFF.
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Red + Blue = Magenta! Set Red to 255, Blue to 255, and Green to 0.
